analysis.one_liner: Makes colleges with high student-loan default rates pay part of the cost of those defaults.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Senator Reed with two Democratic cosponsors in September 2022, the bill was referred to the Senate education committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require colleges whose students repeatedly fail to repay federal loans to pay back a share of the defaulted loan amounts — from 5% up to 20%, depending on how bad the school's default rate is. The money would go into a fund, with part used for programs that help borrowers avoid default and the rest for extra grants to low-income students. It would also count parent PLUS loans when measuring a school's default record, tighten the threshold at which a school can lose federal loan access, and bar colleges from rejecting applicants based on traits linked to default, like coming from a low-income family.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers get better default-prevention counseling and services at high-default schools; Pell-eligible low-income students get supplemental grants from the fund; and taxpayers bear less of the cost when loans go unpaid.

how_it_helps.text: Colleges with a cohort default rate of 5% or higher, or a repayment rate at or below 50%, would owe the Education Department a payment equal to 5–20% of the total amount owed on defaulted loans by their students [S2] [S3].

At least half of the collected payments would fund extra grants to students eligible for Pell Grants at schools that participate in the loan program but are not themselves subject to risk-sharing payments [S3].

The bill would count Federal Direct PLUS loans — including parent loans — in a school's default-rate calculation starting with borrowers entering repayment in 2024, and would lower the default-rate threshold for losing federal loan access from 10% to 5% [S3].

Schools could reduce or waive their payments by adopting an approved student loan management plan with individualized financial aid counseling, and the bill prohibits denying admission or aid based on a student's default risk factors [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities with high default rates or weak repayment records — especially schools that enroll many low-income students but leave them with debt they cannot repay. Those costs could be passed on through tuition or pressure to enroll different students.
analysis.who_pays_short: Colleges with high loan default rates

drawbacks.text: Risk-sharing costs could be passed to students through higher tuition, or could push colleges to avoid enrolling low-income and first-generation students; the bill attempts to counter this by banning admission denials based on default risk factors and by offering waivers to schools serving low-income students that adopt approved loan-management plans [S3].

The repayment-rate trigger (50% or lower within three years) and the low 5% default threshold could reach broad parts of higher education, including community colleges that serve needy students, though those schools can seek waivers or reductions if the Education Department finds a waiver is in students' best financial interest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: the schools whose students fail to repay would help cover the damage, and the money would be recycled into counseling and grants for low-income students. The design hedges against schools dumping risky students, but enforcement would depend heavily on Education Department discretion over waivers, and the broad repayment-rate trigger means some schools serving poor students would owe payments despite the waiver route.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate's education committee in late September 2022, and the committee took no action before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on September 29, 2022, joined by Senators Elizabeth Warren and Dick Durbin; it was the only support it drew [S1] [S3] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges with high default rates — the for-profit sector above all — avoided any requirement to share the cost of unpaid student loans. Borrowers and taxpayers got no new protection from default.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its institutional risk-sharing framework.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 29, 2022 and never scheduled it for consideration.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it received no floor action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4] [S5].

industries.note: These schools enroll large numbers of low-income students and carry some of the highest federal loan default rates, so the 5–20% risk-sharing payments would fall on them hardest. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against borrowers and taxpayers who currently absorb the cost of defaults [S3].

The repayment-rate trigger (50% or lower) and the 5% default threshold reach beyond bad actors to parts of mainstream higher education, including schools serving needy students. The bill gives those schools a waiver and reduction path if they adopt approved loan-management plans [S3].

Up to half the collected payments would fund contracts and cooperative agreements for delinquency and default prevention and rehabilitation, creating new paid work for counseling and servicing providers whose services would help borrowers stay out of default [S3].
